title: Chapter 21 (V.21.3–5)
subtitle: Psyche wavers in her resolve to kill her husband

notes.label: Paradox
notes.body: Apuleius plants a paradox: Psyche is relicta sola ("left alone") and yet, hounded by the Furiae, sola non est ("is not alone"). Her guilt peoples the empty room.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The paradox relicta sola ... sola non est (‘left alone ... is not alone’) dramatises Psyche’s psychological torment: even in solitude she is crowded by the avenging Furies of her own conscience."

notes.label: Simile
notes.trans: wavers like the swell of the sea
notes.body: Her wavering is compared to the aestus pelagi, the swell of the open sea, and the verb fluctuat ("surges, billows") keeps the water-image alive. Her emotions rise and fall like waves.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The sea-simile aestu pelagi simile ... fluctuat renders Psyche’s indecision physical: like the swell of the sea she heaves back and forth, the verb fluctuat sustaining the watery metaphor."

notes.label: Asyndeton
notes.quote: festinat differt, audet trepidat, diffidit irascitur
notes.trans: she hurries, delays, dares, panics, despairs, rages
notes.body: Six present-tense verbs in three clipped, conjunction-less pairs (asyndeton), each pair an opposite. The breathless rhythm enacts her flickering, contradictory feelings — we feel her mind racing.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The asyndetic tricolon of antithetical verbs (festinat differt, audet trepidat, diffidit irascitur) mimics the speed and instability of Psyche’s emotions; the absence of connectives makes each impulse cancel the last."

notes.label: Antithesis
notes.quote: in eodem corpore odit bestiam, diligit maritum
notes.trans: in the same body she hates the beast, loves the husband
notes.body: The climax of her division: in eodem corpore ("in one and the same person") she both odit and diligit. Bestiam (the monster her sisters described) is balanced against maritum (the husband she loves).
notes.exam: In an exam: "The antithesis odit bestiam, diligit maritum, framed by in eodem corpore, crystallises Psyche’s inner conflict: a single person holds two irreconcilable feelings for the same man."

notes.label: Personification
notes.body: In the ablative absolute the evening itself "drags on" the night (noctem trahente). Time is personified and made to move slowly, drawing out the suspense before the deed.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The ablative absolute vespera ... noctem trahente personifies the evening as slowly hauling night behind it, stretching the moment and building tension before the attempt."

notes.label: Loaded Diction
notes.body: The narrator’s own judgement breaks in: the plan is a nefarium scelus, an "unspeakable crime". The heavy moral vocabulary darkens the scene just as Psyche prepares the lamp and blade.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The loaded phrase nefarii sceleris (‘wicked crime’) colours the narrative with the narrator’s condemnation, heightening the horror of what Psyche is about to attempt."

notes.label: Military Metaphor
notes.trans: having skirmished in the battles of love
notes.body: Love-making is cast as warfare: Veneris proelia are the "battles of Venus", and velitatus is a technical term for the light skirmishing that opens a fight. Spent from his "campaign", Cupid sinks into deep sleep.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The military metaphor Veneris proeliis velitatus wittily figures love-making as a battle, the skirmishing verb velitatus explaining why Cupid now lies defenceless in a altus sopor."

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The narrative cuts straight back to Psyche, named immediately after at. With her sisters gone, the reader's attention is fixed on her alone.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: relicta suggests being abandoned, not just being alone: her sisters have stirred her up and then left her to face the deed by herself.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated f sounds link the Furies that torment her with her wavering, so her fear and her indecision sound like one and the same.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.trans: she wavers … she falters … she is torn apart
notes.body: The present tenses put us inside the moment, so we feel each surge of emotion as it takes hold of her.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.trans: her plan settled … uncertain in her plan
notes.body: consilium appears twice in one sentence, first fixed, then uncertain, which shows how quickly her resolve slips away.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.trans: with a resolute mind … she falters
notes.body: Firm words in the first half of the sentence are undone by unsteady ones in the second, so the sentence itself wavers as she does.

notes.label: Metaphor
notes.trans: she is torn apart by her feelings
notes.body: distrahitur means pulled in different directions, which turns her emotions into physical forces tearing at her.

notes.label: Dramatic irony
notes.body: Psyche has been told her husband is a monstrous serpent, but the reader may already suspect that the "beast" is something very different.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: praeceps describes falling headfirst, so her rush to get ready hints at the disaster she is rushing into.

notes.label: Tricolon
notes.trans: night was at hand … he had arrived … he had sunk
notes.body: Three short clauses set the scene in quick succession, so everything is in place for the deed almost before the reader is ready.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The depth of his sleep is exactly what the plan needs, which makes the sleeping god seem helpless and the moment tense.

notes.label: Psyche
notes.body: Her name is the Greek word for "soul" (it can also mean "butterfly"). Many readers have taken the story as an allegory of the soul's search for love.

notes.label: The Furies
notes.body: Goddesses of vengeance who hounded wrongdoers. Here they stand for Psyche's guilt and fear before she has even acted.

notes.label: Venus
notes.body: Venus is the goddess of love, so Veneris proeliis means love-making. She is also Cupid's mother and Psyche's bitter enemy.

questions: Find three phrases in which Apuleius shows that Psyche is pulled in two directions. Which do you think is most effective, and why?
The passage moves quickly from evening to night to Cupid's deep sleep. Why might Apuleius speed up at this point?

context.body:
The tale of Cupid and Psyche is told in Apuleius' novel the Metamorphoses (often called The Golden Ass) by an old woman, to cheer up a girl held captive by bandits. Psyche is the youngest of three princesses, so beautiful that people neglect the worship of Venus to admire her. In a jealous rage Venus sends her son Cupid to make Psyche fall in love with the lowest of men, but Cupid falls in love with her himself.

Psyche is carried by the west wind, Zephyrus, to a magical palace, where an unseen husband visits her only in the dark. He warns her that she must never try to see his face. Her jealous sisters persuade her that he is a monstrous serpent who will devour her and her unborn child, and tell her to hide a lamp and a sharp razor, wait until he is asleep, and cut off his head. This passage begins as they leave her alone with the plan.
